requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.
verdict_reason: verified high finding(s) backed by receipts: requirement-tests-1, logic-edge-1

checked.what: Existing SourceGenerator tests on head: 169/169 passed, 0 failed
Existing SourceGenerator tests on base: 167/167 passed, 0 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDefaultTests.cs: requirement test fails on base (2/2), passes on head (2/2)
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDownlevelTargetTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGuardTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Regeneration: 222/222 generated files verified by 89 passing snapshot tests on head

findings.claim: Every template wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get generated formatters and resolvers with no attribute. The requirement asks for all generated code to be decorated, and the condition is only allowed where the attribute does not exist. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is in the netstandard2.0 reference assemblies and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it can be applied to classes on both. The exclusion is unnecessary and drops coverage exclusion for a large share of consumers, which do not get the attribute through the generated code.

receipt_plan.detail: Run tests/MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Tests/Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDownlevelTargetTests.cs. It first asserts the attribute type exists in the NetStandard20 and Net472 reference assemblies. It then runs the generator with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined and asserts the generated resolver and formatter symbols carry the attribute. Both tests fail on head. (generated tests: GeneratedResolver_IsDecorated_WhenNetStandard20SymbolDefined, GeneratedFormatters_AreDecorated_WhenNetFrameworkSymbolDefined)

findings.claim: The README says the attribute is only emitted where it is available, 'not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework'. That is factually wrong because the attribute exists on both. The doc therefore states a false platform limitation and records the requirement gap above as if it were intended.

receipt_plan.detail: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDownlevelTargetTests.GeneratedResolver_IsDecorated_WhenNetStandard20SymbolDefined: its precondition assertions resolve ReferenceAssemblies.NetStandard.NetStandard20 and ReferenceAssemblies.NetFramework.Net472.Default. They show GetTypeByMetadataName("System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute") is non-null on both, which contradicts the README sentence.

findings.claim: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard drops the attribute on targets where it already exists. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` has shipped since .NET Framework 4.0 and is part of netstandard2.0, and its AttributeUsage has always allowed classes. So the guard is not needed for compilation. Its only effect is that projects targeting netstandard2.0 (including Unity and multi-targeted libraries) or any .NET Framework TFM get formatters and resolvers with no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. That breaks the criterion 'All generated code is decorated', with no setting to turn it back on. The same guard is copied into every template: formatter, string-key, enum, union, resolver, composite resolver, FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGuardTests.GeneratedFormattersAreExcludedFromCoverage on head with NETSTANDARD2_0 and NETFRAMEWORK. It compiles against netstandard2.0 / net472 reference assemblies with the matching preprocessor symbol. It shows the attribute type resolves, yet the generated formatter classes carry no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

hunches.claim: The `#if`/`#endif` lines are emitted at column 0 with `\r\n` endings, and in FormatterTemplate.cs and StringKeyFormatterTemplate.cs the `#if` directly follows prior output with no leading newline. Preprocessor directives must start on their own line. This relies on the preceding Write ending in a newline. After EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces, TransformUtilities was changed to emit `{\r\n` so the directive does not land on the same line as `{`. That change affects all nested-type output, including nested-type snapshots that have constraints.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests, especially nested generic types with constraints and no-namespace types. Confirm every `#if` begins on its own line and the output compiles.

hunches.claim: The attribute is unconditionally added to every generated formatter, resolver and FormatterCache type. The change has no opt-out. Generated types are internal, so the public API is unaffected. But coverage numbers will change for existing users without their opting in. This is the requirement's stated purpose, so it is not a defect. The unconditional behavior is also explicitly acceptable.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests and confirm that only the attribute and `#if` lines changed in generated files, and that no formatter members were altered.

hunches.claim: TransformUtilities change from "{" to "{\r\n" for constrained nesting types is a behavioral/formatting change unrelated to the attribute; it alters generated output for nested generic types with constraints, a recently churned area, with no explanation in requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun generator snapshot tests and inspect snapshots for nested constrained generic types to confirm only newline changes and still compile; cite [L4] as recent churn.

hunches.claim: The new tests only assert that the attribute text and its guard appear in each generated file. They never compile the generated code under a netstandard2.0 or NETFRAMEWORK define, and never compile it where the attribute exists. A wrong guard symbol or a wrong attribute name that still matches the string constants would not be caught.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/FormatterTemplate.cs:33 swap-boolean: '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' -> '#if NETSTANDARD2_0 && NETFRAMEWORK' in the emitted string, with the test constants left unchanged; the Guard constant would then mismatch and fail. Mutate the template and the constant together to see that no compile-based test fails.

hunches.claim:
The guarded-count assertion accepts only the exact forms '#if...
	[attr]
#endif
' and '#if...
[attr]
#endif
'. The test does not check where the attribute sits relative to the type declaration, so it would pass if the attribute were attached to the wrong declaration. In ResolverTemplate the attribute sits right after the XML doc comment. In FormatterTemplate it is emitted after the nesting-type lines. Placement is unverified.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/EnumTemplate.cs:27 delete-statement: move the attribute block to before 'using MsgPack' or into a position that does not precede the class; expected to survive because tests only count string occurrences.

hunches.claim: The test's TestSource defines no generic, nested-type, or type-constrained cases. The TransformUtilities change from '{' to '{\r\n' for the constrained nesting-type path has no test, and the nested and generic emission paths of the templates are not exercised by the new tests.

The assertion `generated.Count >= 5` is weak. It does not check that each template kind (object, string-key, enum, union, resolver) was emitted, so removing the attribute from one template's output could go unnoticed if some other file satisfies the count. The inner foreach would still catch a missing attribute in any emitted file, but a template that stops being exercised is not detected.

receipt_plan.detail: tests/MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Tests/CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs:62 off-by-one: >= 5 -> >= 1; expected to survive because the loop and count do not identify the template kinds.

hunches.claim: The attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. Consumers targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, although the requirement says all generated code must be decorated. The attribute exists in netstandard2.0 (since 2.0) and in .NET Framework 4.0+. The guard is therefore probably unnecessary and silently leaves a large share of users (multi-targeting libraries) undecorated. Note that the #if symbols are evaluated in the consumer's compilation, so they depend on the consumer's TFM.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile a generated formatter in a netstandard2.0 or net472 project and check whether the formatter type carries [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]. The attribute is available in those TFMs (System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis, mscorlib/netstandard2.0), so the guard excludes them needlessly.

hunches.claim: Requirement says all generated code should be decorated, but the change only decorates formatters, resolvers and nested helper classes, and only on non-netstandard2.0/non-.NET Framework targets. Generated code compiled on netstandard2.0/net framework is not excluded, so the README documents a gap. The guard may be deliberate (derived criterion: attribute must exist or be conditionally emitted), but coverage skew remains on those targets. Also the README claims 'All generated formatters and resolvers' while GeneratedCode/other emitted types (e.g. partial nesting types) are not covered.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the templates: nesting partial types emitted by TransformUtilities.EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces carry no attribute, and netstandard2.0/NETFRAMEWORK consumers get none; compare with the 'All generated code' acceptance criterion.

The existing source generator tests ran on head: 169 of 169 passed, 0 failed. 9 unverified hunch(es) remain without an executed receipt. 4 thing(s) were not checked, including mutation testing; compatibility byte diff (base vs head serialized bytes); tests/MessagePack.Tests and other runtime test suites. By signing off, the signer accepts any defect that only those unchecked paths would have revealed. The change is blocked; signing off is not offered until the blocker is fixed.
narrative: This run reviews reading A of REQ-2297 on branch review/ju26-issue-2297/A: Always on, no setting. Every generated formatter, string-key, enum and union formatter, and resolver template (including CompositeResolverTemplate and the nested FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper classes) emits [global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] unconditionally. No GeneratorOptions or MSBuild property is added. This is what the change implements, apart from its #if target guard.
